title: The Agent Role Contract
summary: A browser-local, downloadable eighteen-field contract for defining an AI agent’s mission, scope, permissions, evidence rules, approvals, escalation, logging, evaluation, failure response, and accountable human owner.
audience: Leaders, operators, and builders turning a named AI agent into a bounded and governable organizational role.
implementationStatus: Public browser-local form with Markdown preview and download; no entered information is transmitted or stored.
documentation: Download the completed or blank contract as Markdown
Have the accountable owner approve and maintain it

fields.label: Agent name
fields.hint: The recognizable name; optional because the contract, not the name, is the point.

fields.label: Role
fields.hint: The one job this agent holds.

fields.label: Mission
fields.placeholder: e.g. Keep every published output on-brand and consistent.

fields.label: Scope
fields.placeholder: e.g. Review drafts for voice, clarity, and consistency; suggest edits.

fields.label: Inputs
fields.placeholder: e.g. Draft text and the brand voice guide.

fields.label: Data classification
fields.placeholder: e.g. Internal — no personal or regulated data.

fields.label: Tools
fields.placeholder: e.g. The draft document only. No email, no publishing.

fields.label: Prohibited actions
fields.hint: What it may never do. Be specific.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Never send, publish, post, spend, or contact anyone.

fields.label: Output format
fields.hint: The shape of what it returns.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Marked-up draft plus a short list of flags.

fields.label: Evidence rule
fields.hint: What sources or support it must show.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Cite the guideline behind each flag.

fields.label: Confidence rule
fields.hint: When it must say it is unsure.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Flag, do not guess, when a call is subjective.

fields.label: Human approval
fields.placeholder: e.g. Any publish decision routes to the owner.

fields.label: Escalation
fields.placeholder: e.g. Any legal, medical, or financial claim escalates.

fields.label: Logging
fields.placeholder: e.g. Every review and flag, with timestamp.

fields.label: Evaluation
fields.placeholder: e.g. Sampled monthly against the voice guide.

fields.label: Failure response
fields.hint: What happens when the agent breaks.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Stop the workflow and notify the owner.

fields.label: Owner
fields.hint: The accountable human; always a person.

evidence: The intended business role and representative tasks
Applicable data, tool, approval, retention, and escalation requirements
Named human ownership and evaluation records
methodology: Define one bounded role
Specify permitted inputs, tools, and outputs
Prohibit consequential autonomous actions
Attach evidence, confidence, approval, and escalation rules
Assign logging, retention, evaluation, failure response, and a human owner
assumptions: The organization will test the contract against representative work
Permissions and technical controls will enforce the written boundaries
limitations: A written role contract does not itself enforce permissions or establish compliance
Qualified legal, privacy, security, and domain review may still be required

Same brief, answered from mechanism:

A challenger is discounted mostly because it is unfamiliar and effortful to process. Trust here is built in a specific order: first raise processing fluency (simpler mark, one claim, high figure-ground contrast) so the brain reads you as "easy," then use structured repetition to convert that ease into liking via the mere-exposure effect.

Only once you are fluent and familiar does a source-credibility play (specific proof, a named expert, verifiable numbers) pay off. Asserted too early, credibility claims read as effortful and are discounted.

editorialSections.title: Four levers that move perception, and the order they fire in

blocks.text: Brand trust is not one thing. It is a stack of cognitive mechanisms, each with its own lever and its own failure mode when you skip it.
Processing fluency Foundational
The brain treats easy-to-process as safe and true. Simpler marks, higher contrast, one clear claim: read faster, judged more favorably. This is the floor; nothing above works until it's in place.
Mere exposure Compounding
Repetition converts fluency into liking, largely below awareness. Consistency is not a style preference. Each identical encounter is processed a fraction faster, and that ease is felt as preference.
Source credibility Conditional
Specific, verifiable proof and named expertise raise trust, but only once you are already fluent and familiar. Loud claims from an unfamiliar source are effortful, and effort is discounted.
Affect heuristic Fast & first
A quick "good/bad" feeling forms before deliberation and biases everything after it. Aesthetic ease pre-loads that feeling, which is why craft is a trust input, not decoration.

editorialSections.title: Every trust claim, traced to a real mechanism

blocks.text: The rigor is the product. Each claim carries the named cognitive mechanism, a real concept from the consumer-neuroscience and cognitive-psychology literature, and a confidence rating, so a creative decision can be defended, not just asserted.

cells.text: Easier-to-process brands are judged more favorably and feel more true
Processing fluency: ease of processing raises evaluative + truth judgments (Reber, Schwarz & Winkielman)
Aesthetic ease (simplicity, contrast, prototypicality) drives liking
Fluency & aesthetic pleasure: "beauty in the perceiver's processing experience" (Reber et al., 2004)
Mere-exposure effect: repeated exposure raises liking, via fluency (Zajonc, 1968)
Perceptual + conceptual fluency lift brand evaluation specifically
Fluency in brand evaluation: conceptual/perceptual fluency effect (Lee & Labroo, 2004, J. Marketing Research)
Credible, specific sources earn trust, but effort is discounted
Source credibility: expertise/trustworthiness of source shapes persuasion (Hovland/Yale tradition)
A fast good/bad feeling forms first and biases later judgment
Affect heuristic: affect as a cue in judgment/decision (Slovic, Finucane, Peters & MacGregor)

blocks.text: Verification checkpoint: concept names above are real, established mechanisms in the literature (retrieved 2026-07-04). Effect sizes vary by context and population; confidence ratings reflect that. Treat this as a mechanism map to structure and defend decisions, not a claim that any single tactic guarantees a fixed lift for your brand.
